samples.text:
Nowadays artificial intelligence (AI) can make pictures, songs and even stories in few seconds. This essay will discuss how this change the way people value human creativity and whether we should limit AI in creative industries.

On the one hand, AI may reduce the value of human creativity for some people. When a computer can create a nice painting very quickly and cheap, some customers do not want to pay an artist for many hours of work. For example, a small company may use AI to design their logo instead of hiring a designer. As a result, people can think that creativity is not special anymore. On the other hand, I think many people will value human art even more because it is made by a real person with real feelings and experience. A song which is written by a singer about his own life have a meaning that a machine cannot copy.

In my opinion, there should be some limits on AI in creative industries. Firstly, AI programs learn from the works of human artists, and often these artists do not give permission or get any money. This is not fair and governments should make rules to protect them. Secondly, people should know if a book or a picture was made by AI, so companies must put a clear label on it. However, I do not think AI should be banned completely, because it can be a useful tool for artists to get new ideas.

In conclusion, AI can make some people think human creativity is less important, but others will value it more. I believe that there should be limits, such as protecting artists work and labelling AI products, but AI can still be used as a helpful tool.
samples.why: Addresses both questions with a relevant position · points sensible but underdeveloped · basic linking (On the one hand, Firstly) · simple vocabulary (nice, make) · errors in articles, agreement and word form.

samples.text:
The ability of artificial intelligence to generate artwork, music and fiction has raised important questions about the status of human creativity. In my view, AI is changing how creativity is valued in two opposite directions, and I believe some limits on its use in creative industries are necessary.

On one side, the availability of AI-generated content can make human creativity seem less valuable. Since an image or a piece of background music can now be produced in seconds at almost no cost, businesses may see little reason to commission professional illustrators or composers. When creative work becomes so easy to obtain, the public may start to regard it as a cheap product rather than the result of skill and effort. On the other side, this abundance could actually increase appreciation for genuinely human work. Many audiences value art because it reflects a person's emotions and experiences, and a novel inspired by the author's own struggles carries an authenticity that machine-generated text lacks. In the same way that handmade furniture is valued more highly than mass-produced items, human-created art may become a premium product.

As for regulation, I believe certain limits should be introduced. The most pressing issue is that AI systems are trained on huge collection of existing work, often without the consent of the original artists, who receive no payment. Laws should ensure that creators can decide whether their work is used and are compensated if it is. Furthermore, AI-generated content should be clearly labelled so that consumers know what they are buying. However, banning AI entirely from creative fields would be unrealistic and would deprive artists of a tool which can help with tasks such as editing or brainstorming.

In conclusion, AI may reduce the value people place on creativity in some areas while increasing it in others. Reasonable limits, particularly on training data and transparency, would protect artists without stopping innovation.
samples.why: Clear position on both questions · main ideas extended with apt comparisons, though some generalisation · well-organised paragraphs · good range of vocabulary (commission, authenticity, premium) · rare minor errors such as an article slip.

samples.text:
Now that algorithms can compose symphonies, write short stories and produce convincing portraits, the question of what makes human creativity valuable has become more pressing than ever. I would argue that AI is simultaneously cheapening some forms of creative work and deepening appreciation for others, and that carefully designed limits on its use are both justified and necessary.

The most immediate impact is economic. Commercial creativity, such as stock illustrations, advertising jingles or product descriptions, is increasingly treated as a commodity that AI can supply instantly and at negligible cost. In these areas, the perceived worth of human skill is clearly falling, and many freelance designers and writers have already seen demand for their services shrink. Yet this is only part of the picture. Art has never been valued solely for its surface qualities; audiences are also drawn to the intention, experience and vulnerability behind it. A song about loss means more when listeners know that its writer has actually grieved. Paradoxically, therefore, the flood of machine-generated content may make work that is demonstrably human rarer and more prized, much as handcrafted goods gained prestige after industrial production became widespread.

Regarding limits, a blanket ban would be neither practical nor desirable, since AI can be a genuinely useful instrument in the hands of artists. However, two forms of regulation seem essential. First, the data used to train these systems frequently consists of copyrighted work taken without permission, so creators should have the right to opt out and to receive fair payment when their work is used. Second, transparency is crucial: audiences and buyers deserve to know whether a piece was produced by a person or a program, which clear labelling requirements would guarantee.

In conclusion, AI is devaluing routine creative work while potentially elevating the status of authentic human expression. Rather than prohibiting the technology, societies should limit its use through fair rules on training data and mandatory disclosure, protecting artists while allowing innovation to continue.
samples.why: Both questions answered with a nuanced, fully supported argument · ideas extended through well-chosen analogy · seamless cohesion · wide, precise lexis (commodity, negligible, blanket ban) · complex structures used accurately and flexibly.
